visibility: A state is visible when an ordinary open, catalog scan, or served subject can observe the entry or result it describes.

primitive.basis: BSD flock on a lock file opened O_CLOEXEC: an exclusive holder blocked a second exclusive request, and the lock was released 2.8 ms after its holder was SIGKILLed (results/platform.json). POSIX record locks (lockf/fcntl) are rejected: the lock silently vanished when the same process closed an unrelated descriptor for the file. flock state belongs to the open file description, so a request through a dup() of a held descriptor is granted rather than refused, while a request on a separate open() of the lock file contends with it (results/lockdescriptors.json).
primitive.unmeasured: Only macOS APFS was measured, and CI runs only ubuntu-latest. Network filesystems can emulate flock with POSIX record locks, which behave like the rejected lockf. The format foundation therefore probes the application home at setup instead of trusting the platform: cross-process exclusion, survival of the lock when an unrelated descriptor for the lock file closes, and no-replace publication; a home that fails any probe is refused as unverifiable.

hierarchy.name: home
hierarchy.protects: layout migration and brief global enumeration for catalog scans and sweeps

hierarchy.name: source_alias
hierarchy.protects: slug claim and alias creation; several aliases lock in ascending slug order

hierarchy.name: repository_store
hierarchy.protects: store directory publication and store records; several stores lock in ascending key order. It is held only for those short steps, never across network work or a long-running Git process such as fetch

hierarchy.name: provider_resource
hierarchy.path: owned by the provider storage plan
hierarchy.protects: binding, snapshot publication, pointer movement, and provider reclamation

side_locks.name: staging_entry
side_locks.acquisition: taken before cache/staging/<entry>/ is created and held by its one owner for the entry's whole life, including network work; every other process only tries it without blocking
side_locks.why_outside_the_hierarchy: It is a liveness marker nobody waits on, so holding it across network work cannot block another operation.

side_locks.name: store_fetch
side_locks.acquisition: tried without blocking by a refresh of a published store and held through its network work, stale-lock cleanup, and the record rewrite; the Git processes that write the store inherit its descriptor, so it stays held while any of them runs, even after the process that took it has died; a refresh that finds it busy reports that another process is refreshing the store and does not wait
side_locks.why_outside_the_hierarchy: It is held across network work, which no hierarchy lock may be, and nobody waits on it. The store lock is still taken under it, briefly, to rewrite state.yml.

rules: No network work, provider process, or long-running Git process runs while a hierarchy lock is held.

Every lock attempt uses its own open() of the lock file. Descriptors are never shared or duplicated between lock holders, including two holders in one process, because flock state belongs to the open file description and a second request through a duplicate would be granted the first holder's lock instead of contending with it.
Hierarchy locks are acquired in ascending rank, and within one rank in ascending key order; a lock is never re-acquired while held.
The home lock is never acquired while any narrower hierarchy lock is held.
Side locks are liveness markers and are only ever tried without blocking.

A store is published and the alias that names it is written by one holder of the source-alias lock and the store's lock, held from the store's publication through the alias commit, so every alias that names a store is written under that store's lock.

Nothing removes objects from a published store: automatic maintenance and gc stay off in its configuration and no operation runs gc, prune, or repack. A reader pinned to a full object ID therefore holds no lock and writes no ref.
Nothing deletes a published store. A store no alias names stays in place until an acquisition of its source reuses it; only the startup sweep of abandoned staging entries deletes anything.
Lock files live under cache/locks/ and are never inside a directory that publication or the sweep renames or deletes.

After acquiring any lock, the holder compares the locked descriptor's fstat with the path's lstat (device and inode) and releases and retries on a mismatch, because a sweep may have removed and recreated the lock file.
Liveness is decided by trying the entry's lock, not by age: a crashed holder releases within milliseconds, while no age can distinguish a slow clone from a dead one.

A refresh fetches into a published store only while it holds that store's fetch lock, and the Git processes that write the store inherit that lock, so it is held for exactly as long as a writer lives. Stale packed-refs.lock and refs/**.lock files and temporary objects and packs a killed Git left behind are therefore removed under it before the next fetch. Its fetch updates every ref atomically or none, a stale ref that clashes with that transaction is pruned in a separate deleting step first, and only the record rewrite that follows takes the store lock.

sequences.why: Enumerate briefly, stage without locks, then publish the store and its alias under the alias and store locks.
Ascending rank, and ascending keys within a rank.
A lock may be taken again after release.

Keys within a rank must ascend.
The home lock is never taken while holding a narrower lock.
There is no checkout lock; a local checkout is never a lock target.

publication.rule: The owning hierarchy lock is held, the target path is verified absent with lstat, and the staged directory or record is renamed into place; that check under the lock is the guarantee, because every Metabrowser writer of the path takes the same lock.
publication.defense_in_depth: Where the platform offers an atomic no-replace rename it is used for the same rename: renameat2 with RENAME_NOREPLACE on Linux and renamex_np with RENAME_EXCL on macOS, called through ctypes with no new dependency. It turns a violated lock discipline into an error instead of a silent replacement.
publication.basis: On APFS os.rename replaced an existing empty directory, os.rename onto a non-empty directory failed with ENOTEMPTY, and renamex_np with RENAME_EXCL refused an existing empty directory with EEXIST (results/platform.json). renameat2 was not measured.

nothing_to_recover.action: No durable state changed before the crash.

staging_swept.action: The startup sweep finds the staging entry's lock free and deletes the entry. A SIGKILLed clone leaves its destination and a temporary pack behind (results/concurrency.json), so staging is never inside a published path.

unreferenced_store_kept.action: The crash released the acquisition's locks after its store was published and before its alias was. A published store that no alias names is not visible. It stays in place, and the next acquisition of the same source reuses it and publishes the alias.

sweep_restarts.action: The sweep is idempotent and runs again at the next startup.

fetch_interrupted.action: The atomic fetch moved every ref or none, and objects it wrote stay unreferenced. A killed Git can leave packed-refs.lock, refs/**.lock, a temporary loose object, or a temporary pack; the next refresh removes them under the store's fetch lock before it fetches, which it can take only once no Git from the interrupted refresh is alive. state.yml still records the previous fetch.

prune_interrupted.action: Some refs whose branch or tag the origin deleted are gone and others are not; each deletion is whole, and no commit is removed. The next refresh prunes the rest.

record_behind.action: The refs moved but state.yml still names the previous default revision and fetch time. Nothing reads the record to find a commit, and the next refresh rewrites it.

transitions.effect: Take cache/locks/staging/<entry>.lock, then create cache/staging/<entry>/ on the cache filesystem.

Under the same two locks, a concurrent acquisition had published the same deterministic store first; its records validate, and staging is deleted after the locks are released.
Still under both locks, atomically create sources/<slug>/ with source.yml and store-alias.yml as the sole visibility commit; release both locks.

Remove packed-refs.lock, refs/**.lock, temporary loose objects, and temporary packs a killed Git left in the store. Every writer of the store holds this lock, through the descriptor it inherited, so none of them is live.
git ls-remote --symref -- origin HEAD records which branch the origin's HEAD names.
Typed failure; under the store lock, state.yml records a failed refresh and keeps the previous fetch time and default revision.
git fetch --prune --atomic --no-write-fetch-head origin with the branch and tag refspecs, in Git's own process group, holding the inherited fetch lock.

Git ran and failed, and no ref moved. One transaction cannot delete side and create side/x, or rename Topic to topic on a case-insensitive file system, and Git words that refusal differently for loose refs, packed refs, and reftable, or pushes it past the bounded stderr, so every such failure is followed by the prune.

Git could not start or was stopped at its deadline, which a prune cannot help. No ref moved, because the fetch is atomic; under the store lock, state.yml records the failed refresh and keeps the previous fetch time and default revision.
git remote prune with the mirror refspecs deletes the refs whose branch or tag the origin no longer has, and nothing else; the atomic fetch then runs once more.

The prune may have deleted some stale refs before it failed. Under the store lock, state.yml records the failed refresh with the origin's default branch or the one recorded before, whichever the mirror still has, and keeps the previous fetch time.
Git's process group is killed; each ref deletion is whole, stale refs already deleted stay deleted, and the record is left as it was.
With the stale refs gone, every branch and tag moved together. No object was removed.

The second transaction moved no ref, but the prune deleted stale refs. Under the store lock, state.yml records the failed refresh with the origin's default branch or the one recorded before, whichever the mirror still has, and keeps the previous fetch time.
Git's process group is killed; the second transaction moved every ref or none, stale refs the prune deleted stay deleted, and the record is left as it was.
Git's process group is killed, by the lifespan's cancellation or by the command's immediate exit; the atomic fetch moved every ref or none, and the record is left as it was.
Every branch and tag moved together; branches and tags deleted upstream were pruned. No object was removed.
The origin's default branch is missing from the mirror or is not a commit; the failure is recorded under the store lock.
Under the store lock, state.yml gets the default branch, its commit, the fetch time, and the succeeded outcome; then both locks are released.
